extracted.intended_audience: NSF proposal reviewers, program officers, and proposal submitters (applicants)
extracted.subtask_short: NSF merit review for research proposals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on NSF's 2024-2025 merit review process for evaluating research proposals, including the two formal review criteria (Intellectual Merit and Broader Impacts), the five review elements applied to each criterion, procedural changes, and review stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual Merit
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is one of NSF's two formal merit review criteria. Reviewers evaluate the extent to which the proposed activity can advance knowledge and understanding. The five review elements (potential, creativity/transformative concepts, plan quality, assessment mechanism, and qualifications/resources) are asked with respect to Intellectual Merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broader Impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: The potential to benefit society and contribute to the achievement of specific, desired societal outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the second formal merit review criterion. Reviewers evaluate the extent to which the proposed activity benefits society or advances desired societal outcomes. The five review elements apply to Broader Impacts as well; applicants may cite specific desired outcomes (see 'Examples of Desired Broader Impacts Outcomes').

rubrics_metrics.name: Five-element review: 'What is the potential?'
rubrics_metrics.description: What is the potential for the proposed activity to advance knowledge and understanding (for Intellectual Merit) or to benefit society/advance desired societal outcomes (for Broader Impacts)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the primary framing question asked of BOTH criteria. Reviewers assess the magnitude and plausibility of the potential impact stated by the proposal, separately for IM and BI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five-element review: 'Creativity / transformative potential'
rubrics_metrics.description: To what extent do the proposed activities suggest and explore creative, original or potentially transformative concepts?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers judge novelty and potential for conceptual or disciplinary transformation. Evidence of originality and exploration of new directions strengthens this element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five-element review: 'Plan quality and rationale'
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the plan well-reasoned, well-organized, and based on sound rationale?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the clarity, organization, and logical underpinning of the proposed approach; look for coherent methodology, feasible timelines, and alignment between objectives and methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five-element review: 'Assessment of success'
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the plan incorporate a mechanism to assess success?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers look for explicit evaluation/assessment metrics, milestones, or other mechanisms that will be used to determine whether the project is achieving its stated aims for both Intellectual Merit and Broader Impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five-element review: 'Qualifications and resources'
rubrics_metrics.description: How well qualified is the individual, team, or institution to conduct the proposed activities? Are there adequate resources?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate PI/co-PI expertise, team composition, institutional support, facilities, and budgetary/resource adequacy to carry out the proposed work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of desired Broader Impacts outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrative societal outcomes that NSF considers desirable for Broader Impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NSF's list of examples: (1) Improving STEM education and educator development; (2) Increasing public scientific literacy and public engagement with STEM; (3) Improving the well-being of individuals in society; (4) Developing a globally competitive STEM workforce; (5) Building partnerships between academia, industry, and others; (6) Improving national security; (7) Increasing the economic competitiveness of the U.S.; (8) Enhancing infrastructure for research and education. These are examples (not an exclusive checklist) that proposers can use to design and justify Broader Impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural rule: Minimum external reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduced minimum external reviewers per proposal: 2 (down from 3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Current rules require a minimum of 2 external reviewers and up to 5. This change is intended to reduce reviewer burden; practical implications include relying more on fewer external reviews when panels are not convened.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural rule: Panel review optional
rubrics_metrics.description: Panel review is optional rather than mandatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programs may choose whether to hold a panel. When panels are not convened, funding decisions lean more heavily on external reviews and program officer judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural rule: Panel summaries length limit
rubrics_metrics.description: Panel summaries are limited to 3–5 sentences under current rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panel summaries should be concise (3–5 sentences). This replaces previous more detailed summaries and reflects a shift to brevity in panel documentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural rule: Emphasis on programmatic priorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Increased emphasis on programmatic priorities in funding decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program officers give greater weight to programmatic balance and strategic priorities when integrating reviewer input into funding recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage 1: External Review expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: External review by 2–5 mail reviewers who each provide a written review and a 1–5 score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: External reviewers submit written critiques and a numeric rating (1–5). Reviews are shared with the applicant after the decision. These external reviews may suffice for evaluation if a panel is not convened.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage 2: Panel Review (when convened)
rubrics_metrics.description: Panel convenes 10–30 reviewers over 2–3 days to discuss proposals, generate a concise panel summary, and recommend a funding category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When held, panels discuss proposals and produce a 3–5 sentence panel summary and a recommended funding category (e.g., Highly Competitive, Competitive, Recommended for declination). Panels provide collective input but are now optional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage 3: Program Officer decision process
rubrics_metrics.description: Program officer integrates external reviews and panel input, considers programmatic balance and strategic priorities, and makes a funding recommendation subject to senior NSF approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program officers have increased discretion; they synthesize reviews, panel recommendations (if any), and program-level considerations when making funding recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: External reviewer rating scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Five-point scale used by external reviewers: E (Excellent), V (Very Good), G (Good), F (Fair), P (Poor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E = outstanding proposal; V = high quality; G = competent, no fatal flaws; F = has weaknesses; P = fundamental problems. External reviewers also provide written justification accompanying the rating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel funding categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Panel-level categorization of proposals into funding recommendation bands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical panel categories include Highly Competitive, Competitive, and Recommended for declination. Panels recommend a category alongside the concise summary when convened.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implications for rubric design and review practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Consequences of 2024–2025 procedural changes for reviewers and program officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed implications: (1) reviewer burden reduction — fewer required reviewers and shorter summaries; (2) increased program officer authority — more discretion in funding decisions; (3) less reliance on panel consensus — external reviews can suffice; (4) pragmatic acknowledgment that elaborate panel summaries don't add proportional value (citing Fogelholm 2012 finding that panels don't improve reliability over averaged scores). These implications should inform how reviewers write concise, high-value reviews and how program officers weigh inputs.
